column8: SUM Five sarsen trilithons (ten uprights, five lintels) in a horseshoe about 13.7 m across, open to the north-east; the tallest, the Great Trilithon at the south-west, stood about 7 m above ground. Drawn from the stone catalogue: stone positions and sizes are surveyed from what stands today, the original complete form is reconstructed from them.
column9: UNC Which stones stood, leaned, lay or had been taken by 1625 is not recorded; the 1625 state is reasoned backwards from Stukeley (1720s), Wood (1740) and Barclay (1895). One tradition (John Aubrey, c. 1665-93) ties the fall of the Great Trilithon to the Duke of Buckingham's digging in 1620; it is a report 45 years later, not a dated observation, and the 1625 phase shows stones 55 and 156 fallen on that basis. The middle trilithon heights are catalogue estimates. The fresh-dressed to weathered handover at 2400 BCE (about 120 years) is conjectural: no source dates the weathering of sarsen surfaces. The handover at year 1 CE is a CONVENTION, not a dated event: losses and falls between the end of use (c. 1500 BCE) and the first drawings (c. 1573 CE) are undated. Roman-period disturbance is recorded at the site, and nothing else is known of when individual stones fell or were taken.

column9: UNC Whether the circle was ever complete is unresolved. Darvill (2012) counts uprights 13, 17, 18, 20 and 24 and 24 lintels as missing and favours historic robbing (the sockets of 13 and 20 are recorded); Ashbee (1998) argued it was never finished; drought parchmarks in 2013 between stones 16 and 21 (Banton et al. 2014) may be stoneholes where expected uprights should be, which would favour a complete circle. The built phases show the missing uprights 13, 17, 18, 20 and 24 and their lintels as HYPOTHETICAL stones. The 1625 phase shows the circle as catalogued (state reasoned from the 1720s surveys). The fresh-to-weathered handover at 2400 BCE is conjectural. The handover at year 1 CE is a CONVENTION, not a dated event: losses and falls between the end of use (c. 1500 BCE) and the first drawings (c. 1573 CE) are undated. column8: SUM On Parker Pearson's interpretation the 56 Aubrey Holes held bluestones from about 3000 BCE, so Stonehenge's first stones were a ring about 87 m across just inside the bank. Shown as 56 small standing bluestones.
column9: UNC CONTESTED. The 2008 re-excavation of Aubrey Hole 7 revived Hawley's idea of stones in the holes, and Parker Pearson (2020-22) argues for stones from c. 3000 BCE; Darvill (2022) holds that they held timber posts or nothing. No stone survives in situ. The stone sizes, count in use and the date of removal (here the start of Stage 2, 2620 BCE) are modelled, not recorded. The Aubrey Holes are drawn as open pits by their own landmark regardless of this reading.

End date: Darvill places the dismantling at the start of Stage 4 (2280 BCE), after the central circle (Stage 3) was added; the lead's brief suggested 2480-2400 BCE: Darvill's account is followed here.

column9: UNC Stage 3: only an arc of five stoneholes is evidenced; that it was a full circle, its radius and its stones are conjectural (a ring of 18 is drawn). Nothing stands in this setting between 2280 and 2120 BCE in the model: that gap is a convention covering dismantling and rebuilding.
